explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. Jesus withdrew by boat privately to a solitary place, but the crowds found out about it. They didn't stay home. They followed Him on foot from the towns (Matthew 14:13). That's a lot of walking for a man who was trying to get a little quiet.

Right, friend. The text says the crowds found out about it and followed Him on foot from the towns (Matthew 14:13). Jesus went by boat, and they went by foot. I've chased a cookie box across a counter before, but this is next level.

Yes, friend. When He stepped ashore and saw a large crowd, He had compassion on them (Matthew 14:14). He went looking for a solitary place and found a crowd instead. I think a lot of us would've sighed, but the text says compassion.

explanations.answer: He sends them back to their towns
explanations.explanation: Not this time, friend. The text never has Jesus sending anyone home. It says He saw a large crowd and had compassion on them (Matthew 14:14). Later He even tells the disciples the people do not need to go away (Matthew 14:16).

explanations.answer: He sails off to another shore
explanations.explanation: Good guess if you were hoping for some quiet, but no. He stepped ashore, saw the large crowd, and had compassion on them (Matthew 14:14). No sailing off. He stays right there with them.

That's it, friend. Jesus saw the large crowd, had compassion on them, and healed their sick (Matthew 14:14). Look at the order there. The compassion came first, and the healing followed right behind it.

Close to something that shows up later, but not here. The counting comes at the end, where the text says about five thousand men were fed, besides women and children (Matthew 14:21). In verse 14, Jesus healed their sick. Nobody's holding a clipboard yet.
Nope, friend. No quiz from Jesus here. The text says He had compassion on them and healed their sick (Matthew 14:14). I know a pop quiz when I see one, and this ain't it.

explanations.answer: Send them to the villages to buy food
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The disciples said, “Dismiss the crowds so they can go to the villages and buy themselves some food.” (Matthew 14:15) They'd looked at the late hour and the desolate place and came up with a plan. I think it was a practical one.

explanations.answer: Keep them here to camp for the night
explanations.explanation: Not what the disciples ask. They say it's a desolate place and the hour is late, then tell Jesus to dismiss the crowds so they can go to the villages and buy themselves some food (Matthew 14:15). Nobody mentions camping.

explanations.answer: Have them fish along the shore
explanations.explanation: Fish do show up in this story, but not like that. The disciples ask Jesus to dismiss the crowds so they can go to the villages and buy themselves some food (Matthew 14:15). The fish come later, and they come from a very small supply.

That's right, friend. Jesus told the disciples, “You give them something to eat.” (Matthew 14:16) He had just said the crowds did not need to go away, and then He handed the job right back to the disciples. I bet they did a double take.

Not quite. The villages were the disciples' idea, so people could go and buy food (Matthew 14:15). Jesus answered, “They do not need to go away. You give them something to eat.” (Matthew 14:16) The job went to the disciples.
Good thought, but no. Jesus said, “They do not need to go away,” and then, “You give them something to eat.” (Matthew 14:16) That “You” was aimed at the disciples. The crowd was just there to be fed.

explanations.answer: Only five loaves and two fish
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The disciples answered, “We have here only five loaves of bread and two fish.” (Matthew 14:17) Notice that word “only.” That's the sound of someone who has done the math and doesn't love the result.

explanations.answer: Only seven loaves and a few fish
explanations.explanation: That's a different story, friend. Here the disciples say, “We have here only five loaves of bread and two fish.” (Matthew 14:17) Five and two, no more. I've seen a bigger stash in my own cookie jar.

explanations.answer: Only two loaves and one fish
explanations.explanation: You flipped the numbers around a bit. The disciples say they have “only five loaves of bread and two fish.” (Matthew 14:17) It was five loaves and two fish. Still a tiny amount for that crowd, but it was what they had.

Right, friend. Jesus directed the crowds to sit down on the grass, and then He took the loaves and the fish (Matthew 14:19). Everybody sat down before a single piece of bread went out. It's like clearing the counter before the baking starts.

Look at the order again, friend. Matthew says, “And He directed the crowds to sit down on the grass.” Only after that does He take the five loaves and the two fish, bless them, and break the loaves (Matthew 14:19). The sitting came first.
That's it, friend. He took the loaves and the fish, looked up to heaven, and spoke a blessing (Matthew 14:19). He gave thanks before anything got handed out. That's a good habit for any kitchen.

Zion is a name for the hill of Jerusalem, and the text doesn't send us there. Here Jesus is on a grassy hillside by the lake, and He looks up to heaven and speaks a blessing (Matthew 14:19). Wrong direction, friend, but it's a good name to know.

Sinai is the mountain where Moses, Israel's leader, received the law (Exodus 19:20). That isn't where we are. Here Jesus looks up to heaven and speaks a blessing over the loaves and fish (Matthew 14:19).
Yes, friend. The text says, “They all ate and were satisfied…” (Matthew 14:20). All of them ate, not just the front rows. Imagine a bakery line where every single person gets to the counter.
That's the word. “They all ate and were satisfied…” (Matthew 14:20). Not just fed. Satisfied. I've served plenty of cookies, and that's the review I dream about.
No waiting around in this verse, friend. The text says, “They all ate and were satisfied…” (Matthew 14:20). Waiting is what the crowd might've expected. Eating is what they got.
Opposite, friend. The text says they all ate and were satisfied (Matthew 14:20). Nobody walked away with an empty stomach. That's a lot of people with full bellies.
They did sit on the grass, but that's not the word here. Matthew says they all ate and were satisfied (Matthew 14:20). The sitting was for getting fed, not for a nap.

Yes, friend. The disciples picked up twelve basketfuls of broken pieces that were left over (Matthew 14:20). They started with five loaves and two fish and ended with twelve baskets. My accountant would need to sit down.
Close, but no. The text says the disciples picked up twelve basketfuls of broken pieces (Matthew 14:20). Twelve, not seven. Count those baskets again, friend.

Not even close, friend, and that's the good news. The disciples picked up twelve basketfuls of broken pieces that were left over (Matthew 14:20). Three would've been a nice leftover. Twelve is something else.

Right, friend. The text says, “About five thousand men were fed, besides women and children.” (Matthew 14:21) The women and children are in addition to the five thousand. So the real crowd was bigger than that number.

Look at the last verse again, friend. It says, “About five thousand men were fed, besides women and children.” (Matthew 14:21) The women and children weren't in the count. They were fed too, on top of the five thousand.
